[[File:Moshe_zakai.jpg | thumb | right | Moshe Zakai (1926 – 2015), who derived the Zakai equation in 1967.]]In [[Filtering problem (stochastic processes)|filtering theory]] the '''Zakai equation''' is a linear [[stochastic partial differential equation]] for the un-normalized density of a hidden state.  In contrast, the [[Kushner equation]] gives a non-linear stochastic partial differential equation for the normalized density of the hidden state.  In principle either approach allows one to estimate a quantity function (the state of a [[dynamical system]]) from noisy measurements, even when the system is non-linear (thus generalizing the earlier results of Wiener and Kalman for linear systems and solving a central problem in [[estimation theory]]).  The application of this approach to a specific [[control engineering|engineering]] situation may be problematic however, as these equations are quite complex.<ref>{{cite book |last=Sritharan |first=S. S. |year=1994 |chapter=Nonlinear filtering of stochastic Navier–Stokes equations |url=http://www.nps.edu/Academics/Schools/GSEAS/SRI/BookCH9.pdf |editor1-last=Funaki |editor1-first=T. |editor2-last=Woyczynski |editor2-first=W. A. |title=Nonlinear Stochastic PDEs: Burgers Turbulence and Hydrodynamic Limit |pages=247–260 |publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] |isbn=0-387-94624-1}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Hobbs |first1=S. L. |last2=Sritharan |first2=S. S. |year=1996 |chapter=Nonlinear filtering theory for stochastic reaction–diffusion equations |url=http://www.nps.edu/Academics/Schools/GSEAS/SRI/BookCH10.pdf |editor1-last=Gretsky |editor1-first=N. |editor2-last=Goldstein |editor2-first=J. |editor3-last=Uhl |editor3-first=J. J. |title=Probability and Modern Analysis |pages=219–234 |publisher=[[Marcel Dekker]] }}</ref> The Zakai equation is a bilinear [[stochastic partial differential equation]]. It was named after [[Moshe Zakai]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zakai |first1=M. |year=1969 |title=On the optimal filtering of diffusion processes |journal=[[Zeitschrift für Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und Verwandte Gebiete]] |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=230–243 |mr=242552 |zbl=0164.19201 |doi=10.1007/BF00536382|s2cid=119763576 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
__NOTOC__

== Overview ==

Assume the state of the system evolves according to

:<math>dx = f(x,t) dt + dw</math>

and a noisy measurement of the system state is available:

:<math>dz = h(x,t) dt + dv</math>

where <math>w, v</math> are independent [[Wiener process]]es. Then the unnormalized conditional probability density <math>p(x,t)</math> of the state at time t is given by the Zakai equation:

:<math>dp = L[p] dt + p h^T dz</math>

where
:<math>L[p] = -\sum \frac{\partial (f_i p)}{\partial x_i} + \frac12 \sum \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial x_i \partial x_j}</math>
is a Kolmogorov forward operator.

As previously mentioned, <math>p</math> is an unnormalized density and thus does not necessarily integrate to 1. After solving for <math>p</math>, integration and normalization can be done if desired (an extra step not required in the Kushner approach).

Note that if the last term on the right hand side is omitted (by choosing h identically zero), the result is a nonstochastic PDE: the familiar [[Fokker–Planck equation]], which describes the evolution of the state when no measurement information is available.
